spec.name: carry_rot_mix_v1
spec.limitations: The dominant failure mode is the 32-bit key: with one known (or chosen) plaintext/ciphertext pair an attacker can run exhaustive search over 2^32 keys, each trial costing only 14 table-free byte operations, so the key is recoverable at trivial cost; if a rotation exposes an algebraic decoupling point, meet-in-the-middle over the two key halves reduces this further. Independently, the three rotation amounts and all public constants are fixed, so differential and linear trails through the chain_add carries can be computed offline, and mismatched differentials across alignment classes may leak key bytes one class at a time. There is no key schedule, no substitution box, and diffusion relies on only three fixed rotations over a 32-byte block, so the construction is weak by present standards.
spec.math: State x in (Z/256)^32 and key k=(k0,k1,k2,k3) in (Z/256)^4 applied by position i mod 4. Each step is a bijection on the byte buffer: add/xor/add_key/xor_key are translations (add_key/xor_key translating byte i by k_(i mod 4)), rol is a bit rotation within each byte, rot_bytes is an index permutation, and chain_add and chain_xor are unit-triangular maps over Z/256 with unit diagonal, hence invertible; the composition is therefore exactly invertible and its inverse is the reversed program with inverse steps. The only source of GF(2) non-linearity is the mod-256 carry in the three addition-type steps; every other step is GF(2)-affine. The rot_bytes steps make output byte i depend on input bytes from all positions and destroy the forward-causal triangular structure that would otherwise permit byte-serial key recovery. Because the rotations are 7, 13 and 19 positions (7 mod 4 = 3, 13 mod 4 = 1, 19 mod 4 = 3), successive key injections land on different position classes rather than repeating the same key byte on the same class. No security property is claimed.
spec.assumptions: Block size is 32 bytes; the four key bytes are used round-robin by position and are identical across every block, with no nonce or IV input; rol operands are bit rotations taken modulo 8; all operands are in 0..255; the attacker may hold known or chosen plaintext/ciphertext pairs under a single fixed key and may simulate the program offline. The engine ignores the operand of key steps and substitutes the secret byte.
